title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: A Mill by the Floss, A Family in Flux

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to live inside one of the great novels of the English language.
George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss — a novel about memory, family, money, and a young woman whose mind and heart are too large for the world that contains her.
Today we begin at the beginning — a mill by a river, a family on the edge of something they can't quite see yet, and a narrator who sees everything.
Joining me for this conversation are three people who bring very different but equally indispensable lenses to great fiction.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who is obsessed — in the best possible way — with how great prose actually works.
She reads sentences the way a musician hears a score — alert to every structural decision, every tonal shift.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions that literature brings to life.
When Eliot writes about debt, inheritance, and the grinding social machinery of provincial life, James tells us exactly how that machinery actually ran.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more classic novels in audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He approaches a novel through its voice — its rhythms, its comic timing, its moments of devastating quiet.
I'm delighted to have all three of you here.
Let's begin with the world Eliot places us in — the Tulliver family, the mill, and a narrator who seems to know rather more about human nature than we might find entirely comfortable.
What strikes me immediately — as a performer — is that this is a novel you can hear before you properly understand it.
The prose has this irresistible forward momentum, but it keeps pulling up short — just when you think Eliot is being straightforwardly sympathetic, she turns the knife.
Take Mr Tulliver — a man convinced of his own solid substance.
Eliot gives us the mechanism of his self-delusion with surgical precision:

"He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance."
Pleasant jokes!
His entire sense of his own financial security rests on — jokes.
That's not just comedy — that's tragedy assembled in a single sentence, and she makes it look effortless.
Oliver has put his finger on the thing that makes the opening so extraordinary — Eliot's narrator is doing double work at every moment.
She is simultaneously inside Tulliver's consciousness — giving us his rationalizations with complete fidelity — and standing at a cool, ironic distance from them.
It's the technique that later gets called free indirect discourse, but Eliot wields it with a precision that still astonishes me.
And look at the portrait of Basset — the parish where his sister's family lives.
"Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than half a curate, also poor."
That accumulation of the word 'poor' — five times in one sentence — is a rhetorical choice of real daring.
She's doing with language exactly what poverty does to a parish — the same diminishment, over and over, until the effect is total.
What Eleanor is pointing to is something that runs through the entire novel, and I think it's worth naming plainly.
Eliot is not simply interested in individual moral failure — she is interested in the social mechanisms that make moral failure almost inevitable.
There's a passage that strikes me as one of the most remarkable pieces of social analysis in Victorian fiction.
The narrator observes that grand villainy — plotting, scheming, deliberate contrivance — is actually quite rare.

"It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations."
Spoil the lives of our neighbours — not destroy, not ruin — spoil.
The word choice is precise and pitiless: it describes the diminishment of a life that still continues, merely depleted.
And when you understand the legal reality of women's property rights — or the absence of them — in this period, that passage becomes almost unbearable.
James, that reading sends a chill through me every time — and I've performed a great deal of Victorian fiction.
What Eliot is doing there is something that separates her from almost every other novelist of the period — she refuses to let her characters be safely wicked.
Later in the novel she does this with the gossip of St Ogg's — the town's collective judgment on Maggie Tulliver.
She writes: "We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
Six words — 'not knowing the process' — and she's demolished every comfortable moral verdict any of us has ever issued.
That's what makes performing Eliot both an honour and a genuine humbling — she is always ahead of you.
I want to come back to something James said about inevitability, because I think it connects to the novel's deepest structural logic.
The narrator in this novel is not a neutral observer — she is a presence with a moral intelligence that is warmer and wider than any single character's.
And what she shows us, again and again, is people living exactly as Eliot describes — 'from hand to mouth, with a small family of immediate desires.'
The tragedy of the Tullivers isn't that they're bad people — it's that they are thoroughly ordinary people in circumstances that require an extraordinary moral reach.
And only Maggie — the one person most constrained by her world — seems capable of that reach.
And that constraint is not merely psychological — it is legal, economic, and institutional in the most concrete possible sense.
The Tulliver household rests on a mortgage of two thousand pounds — a figure Eliot is quite precise about.
One thousand of that is his sister's marriage portion — money owed to a woman who, once married, vanished legally into her husband's estate.
Eliot captures this with her characteristic dry precision — the sister had 'come into the world in that superfluous way characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages.'
The irony is devastating because it is technically — and only technically — Tulliver's own framing we're hearing.
Eliot lets the patriarchal logic condemn itself without editorial assistance.
That phrase — 'condemn itself' — feels like the right note on which to open this novel.
A world so thoroughly constructed that its injustices are invisible to almost everyone inside it — except, fitfully, painfully, to Maggie.
In our next segment, we're going to look more closely at that world — the Dodson family, the rituals of respectability, and the question of what it actually costs to belong.

segments.title: Maggie's Mind: Intellect Against the Tide

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great currents — family, money, the slow grind of provincial life.
But at the centre of it all is a child's mind — furious, ravenous, and hopelessly out of place.
This segment is about Maggie Tulliver's intellect — what it costs her, and what it illuminates.
Eleanor Hartley is here as our literary critic — she's been forensically attentive to how Eliot constructs this portrait of a gifted child from the inside.
James Blackstone brings the social historian's eye — the real-world grammar of class and education that shapes and thwarts Maggie's mind.
And Oliver Trevelyan is with us as always — who hears Eliot's prose as a performer, and I suspect has been waiting to read a certain passage about gypsies and cannibalism out loud.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — what's the first thing that strikes you about Eliot's method in these chapters?
What strikes me immediately is how Eliot gives Maggie's jealousy its full moral weight — without flinching from the ugliness of it.
There's a passage in chapter ten where Maggie is watching Tom favour Lucy, and the narrator tracks the exact mechanism by which affection cracks into cruelty.
The sentence structure does extraordinary work here.
Listen to this:

"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her."
That semicolon is doing everything — the first clause gives you Maggie's idealised self-image, and the second dismantles it with the gentlest, most devastating logic.
Eliot doesn't condemn Maggie — she explains her, from the inside, with this forensic sympathy that is absolutely her signature.
And then Eliot goes further — because the thought of cruelty becomes action, almost immediately.
The passage about pushing Lucy into the mud is one of the most astonishing pieces of comic-tragic writing in English fiction — and I use both terms with absolute seriousness.
Because Eliot hauls in Aristotle — drops a Greek phrase into the middle of a scene about a small girl in a muddy field — and makes it work completely.
Here it is — brace yourselves:

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action; the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud."
"Pink-and-white Lucy" into the "cow-trodden mud" — those two compound adjectives, placed against each other, are just superb comic craftsmanship.
But underneath the joke, we're being told something devastating: Maggie's inner life will always exceed what the world allows her to enact.
Oliver's right to dwell on that structural gap — between passion and available action — because it maps almost perfectly onto the social reality of Maggie's position.
A girl of her class and era had almost no legitimate outlets for ambition, anger, or even curiosity.
And look at what Eliot tells us about her education — or rather, the extraordinary patchwork that substitutes for one.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
She has deduced the meaning of the prefix "poly" from reading the dictionary unsupervised — that is a genuinely formidable piece of independent reasoning.
But no-one has told her the practical facts of life — including that gypsies are not, in fact, well supplied with groceries.
The comedy is sharp, but the point is serious: this child has been handed the tools of abstract thought and left without the scaffolding of ordinary knowledge.
And that gap — between abstract reasoning and practical knowledge — is precisely what drives the gypsy episode into such glorious chaos.
Maggie's plan is perfectly coherent on its own terms — she has been told she is wild and gypsy-like, so logically the gypsies will recognise and receive her.
The narrator captures this with that magnificent compressed phrase:
"her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
"Clear-eyed acumen" — that's not a forgiving phrase, it's an exact one.
Eliot is not sentimentalising Maggie's intelligence — she is measuring it, with all its real brilliance and its real blindspots.
The gypsy episode is also — and I say this with full affection — absolutely terrifying if you're inside Maggie's head.
Her fantasy collapses in what the narrator calls a matter of five minutes, and the reversal is spectacular.
From respected scholar-among-gypsies to — and I need to read this exactly as written:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — that's the detail that makes it genius.
Not immediate murder — gradual cooking, as if even in mortal terror Maggie is thinking precisely and methodically.
That is the funniest and most heartbreaking thing: even her fear is intelligent.
Oliver's point about methodical fear connects to something I find quietly devastating in chapter fourteen.
When Maggie is sent away from Tom's school, we're told how much she had galvanised his learning — not by studying the same curriculum, but by asking questions that broke it open.
She had asked Mr Stelling about the Roman Empire with such persistence that Tom achieved something his lessons alone could never have given him:

"he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
"A dim understanding" — note the irony: Tom's gains are modest, tentative, hard-won.
And yet it is Maggie — denied the schooling, the grammar, the entire formal apparatus — who unlocked it for him.
She is educating the educated child, from outside the room, without credit or continuation.
That image — educating from outside the room — is almost a structural diagram of Maggie's whole life in the novel.
She is always pressing her intelligence against a wall that will not yield — family, convention, Tom's contempt, the town's expectations.
And Eliot never lets us forget that the wall is not Maggie's failing — it is the world's.
That's a phrase worth sitting with — educating from outside the room.
What Eliot has done in these chapters is give us the full inventory of a remarkable mind — its acumen and its blind dreams, its ferocity and its comedy.
And she's done it while being entirely honest about the costs — to Maggie, and to everyone around her.
In our next segment, we'll follow that mind into deeper waters — the books Maggie devours, the ideas that shape her, and the dangerous consolations she reaches for.

segments.title: The Comedy of Provincial Life: Dodson and Tulliver Manners

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're looking at what I'd call the novel's comic genius — the world of the Dodsons and the Tullivers rendered in all its provincial glory.
George Eliot is often read as a tragedian, but she is also one of the great comic writers in the language — and nowhere is that clearer than in this novel.
With us today are three guests who each bring a quite distinct way of reading.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for the architecture of prose is second to none.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will tell us what it actually meant to live inside these provincial institutions.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive — brings the ear of a performer to every page.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because you have a gift for finding where a novelist is writing for the voice rather than the eye.
Where does this novel's comedy live for you?
It lives in the narrator's voice — that is where you find it first and most reliably.
Eliot has this extraordinary gift for the deadpan aside — delivered with perfect timing, as if she's looked up from the page and caught your eye.
There is a passage about Mrs Tulliver — thirteen years of marriage and not a lesson learned — that is, I think, one of the funniest sentences in Victorian fiction.

"Some minds are wonderful for keeping their bloom in this way, as a patriarchal goldfish apparently retains to the last its youthful illusion that it can swim in a straight line beyond the encircling glass."
A patriarchal goldfish.
Two words, and Eliot has anatomized an entire type of human soul — and made you feel a little fond of it at the same time.
That balance — mockery and warmth held in exactly equal measure — is what separates her comedy from cruelty.
What strikes me about that sentence is the precision of the image — it's not just funny, it's structurally exact.
Mrs Tulliver's psychology is a closed loop — she can only swim in the circle she already inhabits — and the goldfish makes that visible in an instant.
And notice Eliot calls it a patriarchal goldfish — that word does a lot of ideological work very quietly.
The comic image is also a social diagnosis — delivered so briskly you almost miss it.
And the marriage Eliot is describing is historically very specific — a middling provincial household where the wife's principal social capital is her family connections, not her own judgment.
Mrs Tulliver cannot persuade her husband because the domestic arrangements of the period gave her no lever to do so.
The comedy is real — but it sits on top of a structure that Eliot never lets you quite forget is genuinely constraining.
James is right — and you see that constraint expressed as farce when Mr Tulliver does the exact opposite of what his wife hopes for.
There's a marvellous moment involving Mrs Glegg — she's been sitting in lofty magnanimity, fully prepared to be gracious — and then Tulliver's letter arrives.
"Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
The timing is impeccable — he even makes the civility sound like an insult.
It's the comedy of irrepressible pride — and Eliot is absolutely delighted by it, even as she can see where it is leading.
What I love is that Eliot lets both characters be right in their own terms — Tulliver's pride is genuine and even admirable, and Mrs Glegg's outrage is entirely understandable.
The comedy comes from the collision between two completely coherent but incompatible systems of value.
That is a much more interesting comic engine than simple mockery.
And then there is Tom — who is himself a kind of walking comic essay on the psychology of self-justification.
The narrator explains, with perfect deadpan authority, that if Tom broke his father's whip by lashing a gate — the whip had no one to blame but itself.

"If Tom Tulliver whipped a gate, he was convinced, not that the whipping of gates by all boys was a justifiable act, but that he, Tom Tulliver, was justifiable in whipping that particular gate, and he wasn't going to be sorry."
The distinction between universal and personal justification — rendered in a child's logic about a gate — is philosophical comedy of the highest order.
And yet that same moral temperament in Tom will eventually prove absolutely crucial to the family's salvation.
That salvation has a specific economic form — and it is worth dwelling on, because it is historically very precise.
Tom's three hundred and twenty pounds represents a small fortune in the context of a provincial mill-owning family facing ruin.
And the fact that he obtained it through his uncle Glegg — the network of family obligation working in reverse, as it were — is entirely typical of how small provincial capital actually moved.
Tom simply announces it:
"I have three hundred and twenty pounds in the bank."
No fanfare, no rhetoric — just the bare, proud fact.
It is the Tulliver temperament — that same willful, uncompromising self-belief — finally operating in a register that produces results.
And of course that same narrator who can be so wickedly funny about Mrs Tulliver and Mr Tulliver also turns around and does something profound.
There is a passage about Maggie cutting her hair — which starts as comedy and becomes something else entirely.

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie — perhaps it was even more bitter — than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
The comedy never crowds out the compassion — they co-exist, in this narrator, with the most extraordinary ease.
That is what makes the novel feel so alive — you are never quite sure whether to laugh or to ache, and often you do both at once.
That tonal complexity is where Eliot's real technical mastery shows itself.
She can pivot from the goldfish to that defence of childhood suffering within a few chapters, and neither move feels like a tonal miscalculation.
Both tones are earned because the narrator's relationship with these characters is always rooted in genuine understanding rather than condescension.
What we seem to be saying is that the comedy in this novel is never merely decorative — it is doing serious work about character, society, and the costs of living inside a particular world.
And Oliver's reading of that passage about childhood anguish reminds us that Eliot holds the comic and the tragic in a single hand throughout.
In our next segment, we'll turn to what is perhaps the most consequential relationship in the book — and ask what Eliot is really telling us about the bonds between siblings.

segments.title: Blood and Belonging: The Rift Between Brother and Sister

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three guests who between them bring craft, history, and theatrical instinct to this remarkable novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is utterly fascinated by how George Eliot builds her effects — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who keeps us honest about what the world of this novel actually looked like from the outside.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone should reasonably have recorded — approaches every novel as a performer first.
Today we're looking at blood and belonging — the bond between Tom and Maggie Tulliver, and the terrible way it fractures.
It's one of the central griefs of this novel — two people who love each other profoundly and are, in some ways, constitutionally unable to survive that love.
Eleanor, I'd like to start with you — with young Tom at school, failing his Latin, and doing something rather extraordinary about it.
Yes — and this passage is one of Eliot's most quietly devastating pieces of characterisation in the whole novel.
On the surface it's almost comic — a small boy defeated by Latin supines, resorting to improvised prayer.
But Eliot is doing something structurally very precise here about the limits of Tom's inner world.
He wants to pray for help, but he's never encountered a precedent for this kind of petition — so he almost can't do it.
That is Tom Tulliver in miniature: not unfeeling, not stupid — but constitutionally unable to move outside inherited form.
And then she gives us the prayer itself, which is — well, it's heartbreaking and funny at the same time.
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
That lowercase whisper — it reads like a child trying to smuggle something past God without quite breaking a rule.
What kills me is the Euclid problem — he has to think about how to pray for Euclid separately, because it's a different kind of not-understanding.
And his solution is magnificent — he asks Mr Stelling to simply stop assigning it.
He sets up for it like this — let me find the line —
"And make Mr Stelling say I sha'n't do Euclid any more. Amen."
The "Amen" landing there — it's perfect comic timing, and Eliot knows exactly what she's doing.
But then — and this is the thing about reading it aloud — you realise the comedy never quite covers the tenderness.
He's been praying for Maggie since she was a baby.
That detail sits there quietly and it undoes you.
What Eliot captures here is also a very specific social humiliation — one with real historical weight.
Tom has been sent to a school designed for a different class of boy — one destined for the professions, for Latin and the law.
His father's aspirations have placed him in an institution that measures him by instruments entirely foreign to everything he actually knows how to do.
Eliot puts it with surgical precision: Tom appeared, in contact with Stelling's world, "uncouth and stupid."
"he, Tom Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid."
That phrase — including his full name — is a small masterpiece of narrative voice.
It tells us Tom is acutely aware that the world has a verdict on him — and he cannot quarrel with it on its own terms.
And James, that connects directly to what happens to Tom's character as an adult — that same incapacity to question becomes something far more dangerous.
Eliot gives us a forensic analysis of Tom's mind — and it is unsparing.
She describes minds like Tom's as ones that can get no sustenance from truth — from complex, doubt-provoking knowledge — and so they feed on prejudice instead.
The passage builds to something I find quite terrifying — let me read it:
"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation."

"It is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton."
A staff and a baton — the same object used to lean on and to strike with.
That image is Eliot at her most compressed and brilliant.
And it lands on Tom by name — "Our good, upright Tom Tulliver's mind was of this class" — said with that narrator's irony that sounds almost fond and is absolutely merciless.
The tragedy is that the prejudice Tom inherits is his father's — it's familial, it's loyalty in disguise.
He tells Lucy he holds himself bound — listen to the language — "by his duty to his father's memory, and by every manly feeling."
"he held himself bound by his duty to his father's memory, and by every manly feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems."
Every manly feeling — it's the most devastating phrase, because Tom means it with his whole self.
He is not a villain.
He is someone whose capacity for love has been entirely captured by a system he did not choose and cannot see.
And this is where Maggie's position becomes genuinely unbearable — legally, socially, not just emotionally.
She has no legal standing to override Tom's authority over family honour.
She can declare independence — and Tom's cold response is essentially: very well, then you are on your own.
And then Maggie herself internalises exactly that logic — she turns it against herself with extraordinary force.
Her speech to Stephen Guest — Eliot gives her this formulation that I find almost impossible to argue with, even when I want to:
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves."
"They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
It is a beautiful moral argument — and it is also, in its rigidity, a form of self-destruction that mirrors Tom's exactly.
That parallel is the novel's great structural irony — Maggie and Tom are more alike than either of them can bear to know.
Both are imprisoned by duty — his to paternal legacy, hers to everyone else's claim on her conscience.
And both, in the end, have renounced the one thing that might have saved them — the freedom to simply want.
Maggie's cry about Lucy at the end of that speech — "she believed in me — she loved me — she was so good to me" — is not just guilt.
It is a person who has absorbed so many other people's needs that she has no room left for her own.
And then there's Mr Tulliver himself — because the father casts a shadow over all of this.
He has a moment with Maggie — a line so short and so final that when I first read it I had to put the book down.
She loves him, she tells him so — and he says:
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Seven words — dialect, tenderness, absolute desolation.
And then, to his wife, the same knowledge, slightly expanded — "we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me."
"we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me."
This world's been too many for me — I genuinely believe that is one of the most perfect expressions of defeat in the English novel.
It really is — and it reverberates forward through everything that Tom and Maggie carry.
The father's defeat becomes the children's inheritance — Tom taking the grievance, Maggie taking the guilt.
We'll take a short break, and when we return we'll look at what the novel does with class and money — and what it means to lose everything that defined you.

segments.title: A Family Undone: Social Ruin and Masculine Collapse

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's great engines of tragedy: the ruin of the Tulliver family, and what it does to every person caught inside it.
We have three extraordinary minds with us for this.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for narrative craft is, frankly, alarming in the best possible way.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in the Victorian world, to lose everything in a lawsuit.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than seems humanly possible, and hears George Eliot's prose the way a musician hears a score.
Let's begin where the disaster begins: with Mr Tulliver, his pride, and his catastrophic decision to go to law.
What strikes me first about these early chapters is how George Eliot constructs the mechanism of disaster with almost comic precision.
The narrator is doing something technically brilliant in the passage about Mrs Tulliver's influence on her husband.
There's a metaphor introduced so casually you almost miss how devastating it is.
"It might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
Now, Eliot immediately undercuts it — the real blame, she says, lies with all the previous weight of feathers.
She's building an ironic architecture that distributes culpability across the whole system — marriage, pride, family allegiance — rather than letting it settle on any one person.
The comedy is doing the moral work.
And the comedy is exquisitely timed on the page, which means you have to time it exquisitely off the page as well.
When I read these passages aloud, I find the narrator's voice has this double quality — warm condescension toward Tulliver, but never contempt.
Then you get to Wakem, and the prose shifts register entirely.
The description of Tulliver's hatred is given to us through free indirect discourse — we're inside his paranoid logic — and it's almost operatic.
And then suddenly you get this gorgeous piece of Tulliver invective, pure vernacular fury:
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
That exclamation mark after 'fellow' — that's not punctuation, that's a man's blood pressure.
Eliot writes the grotesque with genuine affection, and you have to perform it the same way.

What I'd add to that portrait of Wakem is that, historically, the provincial attorney in the early nineteenth century was one of the most powerful figures in a community — and one of the most resented.
Tulliver's paranoia isn't entirely irrational — these men really did shape commercial outcomes.
The novel is accurate about the psychology of the man who goes to law convinced of absolute rightness and absolute victimhood simultaneously.
But what interests me most about this section is what the ruin then does to the children — and especially to Maggie.
There's a passage early in Maggie's suffering that Eliot writes with a kind of philosophical gravity that the satirical mode simply cannot contain.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
That phrase — 'no superadded life in the life of others' — describes precisely what poverty does to a child.
It strips away the consolations of perspective, of history, of continuity — leaving only the naked present.
James, that line stops me every time — 'the soul is made up of wants.'
It's devastatingly precise about adolescence — about what it is to desire intensely before you have the vocabulary for what you're desiring.
And then the narrator does something structurally daring — she turns to address us directly: 'though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair.'
The 'we' implicates the reader in the very condescension that has been crushing Maggie throughout the chapter.
You feel a mild indictment landing — quietly, without fanfare — and it's all the more powerful for that.
And the ruin that begins as Mr Tulliver's catastrophe becomes, by the time we reach Tom, something far colder and more systematic.
Tom is one of the great unsympathetic characters in English fiction — not a villain, which would be too easy, but a man armored entirely in virtue.
When he confronts Maggie about Philip Wakem, the speech he delivers is monstrous precisely because every sentence of it is, by his own lights, correct.
"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you."
"While I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both."
That rhythm of accusation — the repeated 'you have' — is prosecutorial, relentless.
When I read it aloud I have to resist the urge to soften it — but it must not be softened.
Tom's language in that scene maps almost exactly onto the legal and moral vocabulary of the period's conduct literature.
'Respectability' — that word carries enormous institutional weight in the 1820s and 1830s.
It wasn't merely social polish — it was access to credit, to legal standing, to the entire apparatus of commercial life.
Tom genuinely believes he is saving the family from a second annihilation, and in purely material terms, he's not wrong.
The tragedy is that Eliot shows us how the logic of respectability becomes indistinguishable from cruelty.
And that cruelty reaches its full expression when Tom finally disowns Maggie.
He says — and I find this almost unbearable to read without inflection:
"You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends."
"You have been base, deceitful; no motives are strong enough to restrain you. I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me."
'You don't belong to me' — four words that dissolve a sibling bond the entire novel has been built upon.
What makes Tom so structurally terrifying is that Eliot never lets us dismiss him as simply wrong.
He has, in his way, sacrificed enormously for that family name.
And the weight of that sacrifice is what gives the rejection its crushing force — it arrives with full moral authority behind it.
Which is exactly why Maggie's internal struggle in the later chapters is so devastating — she has fully internalized Tom's logic even as she fights against it.
That internal struggle — the passage where Maggie battles herself about Stephen Guest — is one of the most demanding pieces of prose in the whole novel to perform.
Eliot gives us the full engine of a human conscience in motion — temptation, self-justification, then the corrective voice rising against it.
And then she arrives at this image that is so physically exact it almost hurts:
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
'Maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul' — organs.
Not faculties, not qualities — organs.
Eliot makes conscience corporeal.
Betraying your deepest self isn't spiritual failure — it's physical mutilation.
And that image illuminates something about the whole arc of the Tulliver ruin that I think gets underplayed.
Mr Tulliver's disaster is cast throughout as a masculine failure — failure of judgment, failure of pride properly managed.
But the costs are disproportionately borne by women — Mrs Tulliver, and above all Maggie.
The social machine grinds on with its own momentum, and those with the least power absorb the most damage.
Eliot understood that in a way that was, for 1860, almost scandalous to say plainly.
That point — about who pays the price for masculine pride and masculine failure — feels like exactly the right place to pause.
We've moved from the comic scaffolding of the camel's back to the shattering 'you don't belong to me,' and seen how Eliot builds both into the same architecture of ruin.
In our next segment, we'll turn to what the novel does with memory and longing — and why Eliot insists the past is never simply past.

segments.title: Eliot's Narrative Art: Distance, Irony, and Sympathy

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
This is a show about one of the greatest novels in the English language — George Eliot's story of Maggie Tulliver, the river, and everything that pulls a person under.
Each episode we take a single strand of the novel and pull it until it gives us something worth thinking about.
Today we're looking at something that makes this novel uniquely itself: Eliot's narrative voice — the distance it keeps, the irony it wields, and the extraordinary sympathy it extends.
With me are three people who have thought hard and long about this book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads fiction the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — she wants to know exactly how it works.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who keeps us honest about what the world of the novel actually was — the institutions, the money, the law.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score, and he is never wrong about the rhythm.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because the novel opens with one of the most audacious narrative tricks I know.
It really is audacious — and it's easy to miss how radical it is on a first reading.
The novel opens with what feels like pure sensory description — the mill, the river, the cold February light.
You're drawn in completely, you believe you're there — and then Eliot pulls the rug.
Listen to what she does:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The whole opening was a dream — a reverie in a chair.
In one sentence, Eliot establishes that memory and imagination are the medium this novel will work in — not documentary realism, but felt, bodily recollection.
And notice the physical detail — the benumbed arms, the elbows pressed on the chair.
That's not decorative. That's Eliot insisting that nostalgia has a body.
That 'Ah' at the beginning — that single syllable — is doing enormous work.
When you perform it, you have to catch yourself — there's a slight startlement in it, someone surfacing from deep water.
And what strikes me is how immediately the voice becomes companionable — 'I was going to tell you.'
Not 'the reader' — you. It's intimate and slightly conspiratorial.
There's also a lovely slight comedy in it — this grand narrator, and she's been dozing off in her chair.
I'd add one thing to what Eleanor said about memory having a body.
That opening establishes a temporal distance — 'many years ago' — which is not merely atmospheric.
It positions the narrator as someone who has survived the story, which gives everything that follows — all the ruin, all the loss — a particular weight.
We are being told this by someone who knows the ending. That is not a small thing.
James, that's exactly right — and it connects to something Eliot does later that I find almost philosophically startling.
When Tulliver is trapped into borrowing from Wakem's client — a man he has sworn to avoid — Eliot reaches for a classical frame.
She writes:
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
She's not being ironic about Tulliver — she means it.
This provincial miller is placed in the lineage of tragic heroes — and the audacity is that Eliot makes it stick.
It works because the novel has already shown us that external circumstance genuinely does bear down on Tulliver in ways he cannot control.
The Oedipus comparison is extraordinary to read aloud — you feel the slight shock of the classical name against the provincial setting.
But what I love is that it's also — quietly — rather funny.
Tulliver stomps around insisting he will not deal with Wakem's people — and the world arranges itself so that he has absolutely no other choice.
The cosmic and the comic are operating on exactly the same moment.
It's also worth noting what the passage says just before that Oedipus line — 'not because Mr Tulliver's will was feeble, but because external fact was stronger.'
"not because Mr Tulliver's will was feeble, but because external fact was stronger."
That is a precise statement about the relationship between individual agency and structural power.
In the real world of this novel's period, small millers were being crushed by exactly that logic — credit networks, legal systems, the concentrated power of men like Wakem.
Eliot is doing social analysis in the form of a sentence. That's not a small thing either.
And then — and this is where I think the novel reaches its most painful and precise psychological work — Eliot turns that same analytical eye on Maggie.
After Tom confronts Philip and forces Maggie to leave, she goes to her room — and Eliot does something extraordinary with her interior.
She writes:
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict."
"And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions."
The rise and fall of that — 'serene heights' to 'hot strife' — is devastating precisely because Eliot gives you both at once.
She sees Maggie's aspiration clearly, and she sees its collapse clearly, without condescension to either.
There's a passage just after that which I find almost unbearable to narrate — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
Eliot describes how Maggie keeps replaying the cruelty shown to Philip:

"Her heart bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
Beat the floor with her foot. Tighten her fingers on her palm.
Eleanor said earlier that nostalgia has a body — well, so does empathy, in Eliot's world.
And the physical specificity is what makes it impossible to read at arm's length.
What I can't quite get past in that scene is what Tom actually says to Philip — the specific terms he uses.
He accuses Philip of having prepared something disguised as kindness:
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you, — from making herself a laughing-stock, — from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son."
Tom is voicing class contempt — Maggie is not good enough — and he thinks he is being protective.
That is the cruelty Eliot anatomises throughout this novel — the violence that believes itself to be love.
And the narrative voice never loses its steadiness in the face of that.
It doesn't editorialize wildly — it shows you Tom's logic from inside, and it shows you its cost from inside Maggie.
The distance and the sympathy operate simultaneously — that's the technique, and it's staggeringly hard to do.
It requires the narrator to hold complete understanding of a character and complete judgment of their actions at the same time — without collapsing either into the other.
And that, I think, is exactly why this novel repays rereading in a way very few do.
The narrator knows more than you — and asks you to grow into that knowledge alongside her.
We're going to take a short break — and when we come back, we'll look at the world this novel is set in: the St Ogg's society that shapes and constrains everyone in it.

segments.title: Closing: The Mill's Flood—Tragedy and Transcendence

utterances.text: We've arrived at the place where all rivers run — the ending of The Mill on the Floss, and the question of what this novel ultimately means.

Before we reach the flood, though, I want to linger on something the novel has been building quietly from almost its first pages: the weight of home, of memory, of love that has no rational justification.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about the way Eliot sets up the tragedy long before the water rises — can you take us in?
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how Eliot plants the seeds of the ending in the most ordinary, domestic moments.
Take Mr Tulliver riding away on his horse — a man who has just made a resolute decision, fully committed, getting on with things.
And then Eliot gives us this extraordinary little moment of hesitation.
She writes that he appeared to be, quote, smitten by some sudden thought — and he turns his horse, and rides slowly back.
And what comes out of him — this man who struggles to articulate anything tender — is simply:
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
Structurally, it's a throwaway moment — he just turns his horse around.
But Eliot has quietly handed us the entire emotional logic of the ending in one sentence.
Maggie's catastrophe will be precisely that: she'll have nobody but Tom.
And the beauty of it, from a performer's point of view, is the dialect.
"Belike" — that single word does more work than a paragraph of standard English ever could.
It's uncertainty, it's tenderness, it's the voice of a man who can't quite bring himself to look his own fear in the face.
When I've read this aloud, there's always a silence in the room after that line.
Not because it's conventionally beautiful prose — it isn't — but because Eliot has found the exact sound of a man's private grief.
And it sits in your chest long after you've put the book down.
What Tulliver's fear articulates — without his being able to name it properly — is the genuine legal and social precariousness of a woman in that period.
A daughter had no independent standing in law — she could not inherit the mill, she could not sue, she could barely contract.
Her entire future, materially and socially, rested on the goodwill of male relatives.
Tulliver knows this in his bones, even if the novel doesn't deliver a lecture about it.
His turning his horse around is not sentimentality — it is a man confronting a structural reality he is powerless to change.
That word — roots — keeps returning in this novel, doesn't it.

James, before we get to the flood itself, there's that passage about home and memory — the one about the elderberry bush — that feels like Eliot's philosophical foundation for everything that follows.
It is the philosophical foundation — and it's also, if you read it carefully, a quiet argument against the Whig idea of progress.
Eliot gives us this apparently cozy meditation on childhood home, and then she sharpens it into something with real intellectual teeth.
She writes — and I want to read this at length, because the rhythm of it matters:

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
"The labour of choice" — that phrase is doing an enormous amount of work.
Choice, in the Victorian liberal economy, is the mark of a free and rational agent.
And Eliot is saying — very quietly — that the deepest attachments of human life precede choice entirely.
They are not chosen. They are grown into.
And notice she allows herself a satirical aside right in the middle of that meditation — something about the British man and the foreign brute.
That's the Eliot move I find most thrilling — the sudden flash of irony inside a deeply earnest passage.
It keeps you from getting maudlin, keeps the narrator's intelligence present on the page, so that when the emotion does land, you trust it.
She earns the elderberry bush precisely because she's made fun of the person who would dismiss it.
Speaking of people who would dismiss things — I must put in a word for Bob Jakin, who is to this novel what Falstaff is to Henry the Fourth.
Not the tragic hero — the one who keeps reminding you the world is also ridiculous and alive.
There's this scene with Bob and Mrs Glegg — Bob selling figured muslin — and it is a masterpiece of comic manipulation.
He says, of a piece of damaged muslin:
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
He's insulting her and flattering her and selling her simultaneously — it's a triple-bank shot of class comedy.
And Eliot writes it entirely without footnotes — you just hear the music of the thing and you know exactly what's happening.
Bob, of course, is the one who saves Maggie after the scandal — and that matters enormously.
Eliot gives her redemption — if you can call it that — not from the respectable classes, but from the peddler.
Which brings us, finally, to Maggie herself — and to the passage that might be the most quietly devastating in the whole novel.
Eleanor, that moment when Maggie sees her father's helplessness — Eliot describes it as a supreme moment.
It's one of those passages where Eliot reaches the very limit of what prose can do — and then quietly steps past it.
She calls it a supreme moment — one of those moments in life when everything else falls away.
The full sentence is:

"all we have hoped or delighted in, all we can dread or endure, falls away from our regard as insignificant; is lost, like a trivial memory, in that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
"Simple, primitive love" — she doesn't say noble, she doesn't say elevated.
She says primitive — pre-rational, pre-social, the oldest thing in us.
And "knits" — that verb is extraordinary.
Not binds, not chains — knits.
Something woven together, something domestic and patient and made from repetition.
And that's what the flood does, structurally.
It strips everything away — the respectability, the scandals, the lawsuits, the money — and leaves only that primitive thing.
Maggie rows to Tom not because he has been good to her — he hasn't, not really — but because he is the person who was there at the beginning.
Eliot refuses to make that either simple heroism or simple folly.
It is just the truth of how love actually works, which is far more disturbing than either.
When I've read the ending aloud — and I've done it many times — I find I have to prepare for it the way you prepare for a difficult piece of music.
Because Eliot gives you almost nothing to hide behind.
The prose is stripped back, the sentences shorten — and you feel the current, the real one, in the rhythm.
Tom says "Maggie" — and you hear, in that single word, everything he has never managed to say to her.
And then it's over.
That's what great tragedy does — it gives you the thing you've been waiting for, and takes it away in the same breath.
On that note — and I can think of no better one — it seems right to close this conversation where the novel closes: in a kind of stillness after enormous movement.
Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you.
You've made this novel feel as alive today as it was in 1860.
For listeners who've come this far with us: the mill still stands, the river still runs, and Eliot's voice is still in the water.
Thank you for joining The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c8:p6.text:
For Mr Tulliver was in a position neither new nor striking, but, like other
everyday things, sure to have a cumulative effect that will be felt in the
long run: he was held to be a much more substantial man than he really was. And
as we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us, it was his habit
to think of failure and ruin with the same sort of remote pity with which a
spare, long-necked man hears that his plethoric short-necked neighbour is
stricken with apoplexy. He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about
his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of
land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of
considerable substance. They gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a
market-day, and if it had not been for the recurrence of half-yearly payments,
Mr Tulliver would really have forgotten that there was a mortgage of two
thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold. That was not altogether his own
fault, since one of the thousand pounds was his sister’s fortune, which
he had to pay on her marriage; and a man who has neighbours that  will  go
to law with him is not likely to pay off his mortgages, especially if he enjoys
the good opinion of acquaintances who want to borrow a hundred pounds on
security too lofty to be represented by parchment. Our friend Mr Tulliver had
a good-natured fibre in him, and did not like to give harsh refusals even to
his sister, who had not only come in to the world in that superfluous way
characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages, but had quite
thrown herself away in marriage, and had crowned her mistakes by having an
eighth baby. On this point Mr Tulliver was conscious of being a little weak;
but he apologised to himself by saying that poor Gritty had been a good-looking
wench before she married Moss; he would sometimes say this even with a slight
tremulousness in his voice. But this morning he was in a mood more becoming a
man of business, and in the course of his ride along the Basset lanes, with
their deep ruts,—lying so far away from a market-town that the labour of
drawing produce and manure was enough to take away the best part of the profits
on such poor land as that parish was made of,—he got up a due amount of
irritation against Moss as a man without capital, who, if murrain and blight
were abroad, was sure to have his share of them, and who, the more you tried to
help him out of the mud, would sink the further in. It would do him good rather
than harm, now, if he were obliged to raise this three hundred pounds; it would
make him look about him better, and not act so foolishly about his wool this
year as he did the last; in fact, Mr Tulliver had been too easy with his
brother-in-law, and because he had let the interest run on for two years, Moss
was likely enough to think that he should never be troubled about the
principal. But Mr Tulliver was determined not to encourage such shuffling
people any longer; and a ride along the Basset lanes was not likely to enervate
a man’s resolution by softening his temper. The deep-trodden hoof-marks,
made in the muddiest days of winter, gave him a shake now and then which
suggested a rash but stimulating snarl at the father of lawyers, who, whether
by means of his hoof or otherwise, had doubtless something to do with this
state of the roads; and the abundance of foul land and neglected fences that
met his eye, though they made no part of his brother Moss’s farm,
strongly contributed to his dissatisfaction with that unlucky agriculturist. If
this wasn’t Moss’s fallow, it might have been; Basset was all
alike; it was a beggarly parish, in Mr Tulliver’s opinion, and his
opinion was certainly not groundless. Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a
poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than
half a curate, also poor. If any one strongly impressed with the power of the
human mind to triumph over circumstances will contend that the parishioners of
Basset might nevertheless have been a very superior class of people, I have
nothing to urge against that abstract proposition; I only know that, in point
of fact, the Basset mind was in strict keeping with its circumstances. The
muddy lanes, green or clayey, that seemed to the unaccustomed eye to lead
nowhere but into each other, did really lead, with patience, to a distant
high-road; but there were many feet in Basset which they led more frequently to
a centre of dissipation, spoken of formerly as the “Markis o’
Granby,” but among intimates as “Dickison’s.” A large
low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected
beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy
pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night’s
guttered candle,—all this may not seem a very seductive form of
temptation; but the majority of men in Basset found it fatally alluring when
encountered on their road toward four o’clock on a wintry afternoon; and
if any wife in Basset wished to indicate that her husband was not a
pleasure-seeking man, she could hardly do it more emphatically than by saying
that he didn’t spend a shilling at Dickison’s from one Whitsuntide
to another. Mrs Moss had said so of  her  husband more than once, when
her brother was in a mood to find fault with him, as he certainly was to-day.
And nothing could be less pacifying to Mr Tulliver than the behaviour of the
farmyard gate, which he no sooner attempted to push open with his riding-stick
than it acted as gates without the upper hinge are known to do, to the peril of
shins, whether equine or human. He was about to get down and lead his horse
through the damp dirt of the hollow farmyard, shadowed drearily by the large
half-timbered buildings, up to the long line of tumble-down dwelling-houses
standing on a raised causeway; but the timely appearance of a cowboy saved him
that frustration of a plan he had determined on,—namely, not to get down
from his horse during this visit. If a man means to be hard, let him keep in
his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and
with the command of a distant horizon. Mrs Moss heard the sound of the
horse’s feet, and, when her brother rode up, was already outside the
kitchen door, with a half-weary smile on her face, and a black-eyed baby in her
arms. Mrs Moss’s face bore a faded resemblance to her brother’s;
baby’s little fat hand, pressed against her cheek, seemed to show more
strikingly that the cheek was faded.
c8:p6.summary: The narrator exposes Mr Tulliver's false sense of security despite carrying a two-thousand-pound mortgage, his unconscious blindness to his sister's suffering, and his weakness in lending to Moss; the passage then provides a scathing sociological portrait of Basset parish, its poor soil, poverty, and the temptations of Dickison's public house.
c8:p6.best_quote: He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance.

c3:p79.text:
Plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance, in order to compass a selfish
end, are nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist: they demand too
intense a mental action for many of our fellow-parishioners to be guilty of
them. It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so
much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial
falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by
small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised
insinuations. We live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of
immediate desires; we do little else than snatch a morsel to satisfy the hungry
brood, rarely thinking of seed-corn or the next year’s crop.
c3:p79.summary: The narrator offers profound reflection that most moral failures result not from deliberate villainy but from small, thoughtless acts, lazy compliance, and accumulated minor dishonestries.

It was soon known throughout St Ogg’s that Miss Tulliver was come back;
she had not, then, eloped in order to be married to Mr Stephen Guest,—at
all events, Mr Stephen Guest had not married her; which came to the same
thing, so far as her culpability was concerned. We judge others according to
results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived
at. If Miss Tulliver, after a few months of well-chosen travel, had returned as
Mrs Stephen Guest, with a post-marital  trousseau , and all the
advantages possessed even by the most unwelcome wife of an only son, public
opinion, which at St Ogg’s, as else where, always knew what to think,
would have judged in strict consistency with those results. Public opinion, in
these cases, is always of the feminine gender,—not the world, but the
world’s wife; and she would have seen that two handsome young
people—the gentleman of quite the first family in St
Ogg’s—having found themselves in a false position, had been led
into a course which, to say the least of it, was highly injudicious, and
productive of sad pain and disappointment, especially to that sweet young
thing, Miss Deane. Mr Stephen Guest had certainly not behaved well; but then,
young men were liable to those sudden infatuated attachments; and bad as it
might seem in Mrs Stephen Guest to admit the faintest advances from her
cousin’s lover (indeed it  had  been said that she was actually
engaged to young Wakem,—old Wakem himself had mentioned it), still, she
was very young,—“and a deformed young man, you know!—and
young Guest so very fascinating; and, they say, he positively worships her (to
be sure, that can’t last!), and he ran away with her in the boat quite
against her will, and what could she do? She couldn’t come back then; no
one would have spoken to her; and how very well that maize-coloured satinette
becomes her complexion! It seems as if the folds in front were quite come in;
several of her dresses are made so,—they say he thinks nothing too
handsome to buy for her. Poor Miss Deane! She is very pitiable; but then there
was no positive engagement; and the air at the coast will do her good. After
all, if young Guest felt no more for her than  that  it was better for her
not to marry him. What a wonderful marriage for a girl like Miss
Tulliver,—quite romantic? Why, young Guest will put up for the borough at
the next election. Nothing like commerce nowadays! That young Wakem nearly went
out of his mind; he always  was  rather queer; but he’s gone abroad
again to be out of the way,—quite the best thing for a deformed young
man. Miss Unit declares she will never visit Mr and Mrs Stephen
Guest,—such nonsense! pretending to be better than other people. Society
couldn’t be carried on if we inquired into private conduct in that
way,—and Christianity tells us to think no evil,—and my belief is,
that Miss Unit had no cards sent her.”
c55:p0.summary: The narrator ironically explains how St Ogg's society would have accepted Maggie's elopement had she returned as Mrs Stephen Guest, revealing how public opinion judges by outcomes rather than moral truth.
c55:p0.best_quote: We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at.

Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
